notions.question: How do you express obligation, possibility or politeness with English modal verbs?
notions.definition: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) are followed by the bare infinitive without “to”, take no -s in the third person and form the negative and the interrogative on their own. They express degrees of possibility (may, might, could), obligation (must; have to for an external obligation; “mustn't” = prohibition, “don't have to” = absence of obligation), advice (should), ability (can, could), polite requests (could you, would you), willingness or the future (will, would). In business correspondence, could and would soften requests; shall expresses obligation in contracts.

lignes: Could you send us a sample?
Invoices must be paid within 30 days.
You don't have to pay a deposit.
The Seller shall deliver the goods.

exemple.texte: “We would be grateful if you could confirm the order. The goods must be delivered by 15 December. You don't have to sign the delivery note in person.”

confusions.explication: A common misinterpretation among French speakers.

verification: Translate: « Vous n'êtes pas obligé de payer d'acompte » and « Vous ne devez pas divulguer le prix ».

notions.question: When and how should you use the passive in professional English?
notions.definition: The passive is formed with be conjugated in the required tense + past participle (The goods were shipped). It puts the emphasis on the action or its result rather than on the agent, which is introduced by “by” if it is mentioned. It is frequent in professional and technical writing (processes, reports, procedures) and makes it possible to avoid assigning blame (“Mistakes were made”). English also allows the passive with an indirect object turned into the subject (“We were sent the wrong items”), where French often uses « on ».

termes.definition: Construction in which the subject undergoes the action.
The doer of the action in a passive sentence.

exemple.texte: “Your order has been received and will be processed within 48 hours. You will be informed as soon as the goods are dispatched.”

confusions.explication: English makes the recipient the subject of the passive.

verification: Put into the passive: “We will deliver the goods next week.”

notions.question: How do you express a condition and its consequences in English?
notions.definition: English distinguishes several types of conditional sentences. Type 1 (real / likely): if + present, will + base form (If you order 500 units, we will give you a 5% discount). Type 2 (hypothetical): if + simple past, would + base form (If we lowered our prices, we would sell more). Type 3 (unreal past): if + past perfect, would have + past participle (If you had paid on time, we would have delivered). Unlike French, “will” and “would” are never used in the clause introduced by “if” (except polite “would”: If you would kindly…). “Should you need” is an elegant replacement for “if you need”. Unless = except if.

exemple.texte: “If you confirm your order by Friday, we will ship it on Monday. Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact us. Unless payment is received within ten days, we shall suspend deliveries.”

confusions.explication: No will in the if-clause (except in special cases).

verification: Complete: “If we ___ (receive) your payment, we ___ (ship) the goods.”

notions.question: When should you use the present perfect rather than the simple past?
notions.definition: The simple past places an action in a finished, dated past (We shipped the goods last week / in 2024 / on Monday). The present perfect (have + past participle) links the past to the present: a present result, a review up to now, a duration that continues (We have received your order; Sales have risen this year; We have worked with them since 2015 / for ten years). The markers “yesterday, last, ago, in 2020” call for the simple past; “since, for (ongoing duration), already, yet, so far, recently, this year” call for the present perfect. The French passé composé can therefore be translated by either tense.

exemple.texte: « Nous travaillons avec eux depuis 2018 » → “We have worked (have been working) with them since 2018”, not “We work with them since 2018”.

confusions.explication: A common mistake among French speakers.

verification: Translate: « Les ventes ont augmenté l'an dernier » and « Les ventes ont augmenté cette année ».

questions.enonce: “You don't have to sign the form” means:

choix.texte: There is no obligation for you to sign the form
You are forbidden to sign the form
You are unable to sign
You did not sign

questions.enonce: Put into the passive: “The forwarder has booked the container.”

choix.texte: The container has been booked by the forwarder.
choix.explication: Present perfect passive: has been + past participle.

choix.texte: The container was booked by the forwarder.
The container has booked by the forwarder.
The container is booking by the forwarder.
If you order 1,000 units, we will offer a discount.
choix.explication: Type 1: if + present, will + base form.

choix.texte: If you will order 1,000 units, we will offer a discount.
If you ordered 1,000 units, we will offer a discount.
If you order 1,000 units, we would offered a discount.

questions.enonce: Translate: « Nous sommes partenaires depuis cinq ans. »

choix.texte: We have been partners for five years.
choix.explication: Present perfect + for (duration up to now).

choix.texte: We are partners since five years.
We were partners for five years.
choix.explication: Implies that the partnership is over.

choix.texte: We have been partners since five years.
choix.explication: Since is used with a starting point (since 2021).

choix.texte: We received your payment yesterday.
We have received your payment yesterday.
choix.explication: Yesterday rules out the present perfect.

choix.texte: We have receive your payment.
We receive your payment yesterday.

flashcards.question: Summarise the useful rules for business English: modals, the passive, conditionals, present perfect / simple past.
flashcards.reponse: Modals + bare infinitive: could/would (politeness), must (obligation), mustn't (prohibition) ≠ don't have to (no obligation), should (advice), may/might (possibility), shall (contractual obligation). Passive: be + past participle, emphasis on the action (Your order has been received). Conditionals: type 1 if + present / will; type 2 if + simple past / would; type 3 if + past perfect / would have; no will after if; should you…, unless. Simple past for the dated past (yesterday, ago, last); present perfect for a link with the present (since, for, yet, already, this year).
indispensables: Simple past and present perfect markers
